summary:
Here's the final summary, 189 words:

---

TwinWorlds scores every land area on Earth by how closely it matches a chosen site on Mars or the Moon. It uses only measurements taken the same way on both worlds: slope, hilliness, day and night ground temperature, brightness, plant cover, ground type, air and minerals. Pick any spot, such as Perseverance's Jezero crater or the Artemis south pole, and two linked 3D globes light up Earth's best analogs. Mission lenses rescore Earth for landing, rover driving, a lunar base or astrobiology. Mission Twin goes further: it finds an Earth route that matches a rover's real drive segment by segment, and the best dates to rehearse it.

Analog sites are usually picked by reputation and described in words. TwinWorlds turns "Mars-like" into a number you can check. In a blind test, without ever being told about them, it ranks the Atacama and Utah's Mars Desert Research Station in the top 1.5% of Earth for Jezero. It also surfaces overlooked analogs, including several in Pakistan.

It is just as honest about what Earth cannot rehearse, such as gravity, thin air and radiation. That helps mission teams test where Earth can stand in, and plan chambers for where it can't.
details:
TwinWorlds finds the places on Earth that best match a chosen site on Mars or the Moon, and shows what Earth cannot match.

You pick a target: a landing site such as Perseverance’s Jezero crater, the Artemis south pole, a NASA mission, or any spot you click. TwinWorlds then scores all 79,625 land cells on Earth (a 0.5 degree grid) against it. Two linked 3D globes show the result. Earth lights up as a heatmap, the best regions are outlined, and “Twin Dive” flies both globes down to the surface together at the same scale and angle.

We only compare quantities measured the same way on both worlds: slope, hilliness, daytime and night-time ground temperature, the day-night temperature swing, surface brightness and plant cover. Each one is scored with a bell curve, with its width set by Earth’s own natural spread. The scores are combined with a weighted geometric mean, so one bad condition cannot hide behind good ones. If a target’s value lies beyond anything on Earth, it does not vote; it is shown as a gap instead.

Mission lenses rescore Earth for a specific goal: landing, rover driving, a lunar base, thermal testing or astrobiology.

Mission Twin takes a rover’s real drive from NASA traverse files, cuts it into 250 m segments, and searches Earth’s terrain for a path whose slopes and climbs follow the same sequence. It then picks the dates and hours when that Earth path’s ground temperature and sun angle are closest to what the rover experienced.

Science panels add more:

  • ground type, from a heat-flow model checked against Jezero’s published values;
  • dust, water vapour and UV shielding;
  • rock chemistry from Curiosity and Perseverance;
  • mineral spectra, comparing CRISM data from Mars orbit with NASA EMIT data from Earth orbit.

A Rehearsability Map colours the whole of Mars and the Moon by how well Earth can stand in for each spot.

Benefits

  • It turns “Mars-like” from an adjective into a number that anyone can check, with the source and the maths behind every value.
  • It points teams to the right Earth site for a specific mission, route and season, not just a famous one.
  • It surfaces overlooked analogs. Several sites in Pakistan rank in the top 2% of Earth for real targets, and none of them is on the usual analog lists.
  • It is open: a free website, a public API, and plain-language and expert modes.

Intended impact

We want field-test planning to start with evidence. Before a rover, drill or crew procedure goes to Mars or the Moon, teams should be able to rehearse it where Earth matches best. They should also know exactly which conditions (gravity, thin air, radiation, ozone-free UV) need chambers or rigs instead. We also hope it opens analog science to countries whose landscapes have never been studied this way.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python (data pipeline and scoring) and JavaScript (web app and API).
  • Frontend: CesiumJS for the 3D globes, Chart.js, Vite.
    • Earth: NASA MODIS, Landsat, EMIT and POWER.
    • Mars and Moon: MGS MOLA and TES, MRO CRISM, LRO LOLA and Diviner.
    • Rovers and missions: Curiosity and Perseverance results, NASA MMGIS rover traverses.
    • Partner and other data: the Mars Climate Database (ESA/CNES/LMD), ERA5 weather, USGS elevation and reference samples, and the RELAB spectral library.
  • Hardware: just laptops. Everything runs in a web browser.

How it is creative

  • Rehearsing a route, not just a place. Mission Twin matches a rover’s actual drive, segment by segment, and tells you when to go.
  • Earth’s limits are part of the answer. Instead of hiding what Earth cannot reproduce, every result shows it, with the hardware teams use to fake it.
  • A blind test proves it. We never told the engine where the famous analog sites are. It still ranks Utah’s Mars Desert Research Station and the Atacama in the top 1.5% of Earth for Jezero, where random chance would give the top 50%.
  • A map of Mars and the Moon by rehearsability. It flips the usual question to “where on Mars can’t we practise at all?”
  • Same instrument logic on both worlds. For example, Mars carbonate seen from orbit is matched against limestone in Sindh, also seen from orbit (r = 0.96).

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty:
    • No made-up numbers; every value carries its source.
    • Modelled data is labelled as modelled.
    • Conditions beyond Earth’s range are reported rather than forced into a score.
  • Bias: high, cold, dry Asian plateaus win often. We measured this, explain it in the app, and added a “Spread worldwide” view that shows the best option on every continent.
  • Validation: the blind test against 14 known analog sites, plus checks of our thermal model against published values.
  • Accessibility: a plain-language Normal mode and a full-maths Nerd mode, a guided Story mode, reduced-motion support, and a phone layout.
  • Responsible AI: Gemini only sees measured numbers and only explains them; it never ranks or scores.
  • Security: API keys are kept server-side and never in the code.
  • Cost: built entirely on free and open data and free hosting, so anyone can use it.|
